title: Nyquist's Stability Criterion
intro: Bode plots look at the loop gain only along $s = j\omega$, which can be misleading when the phase crosses $-180^{\circ}$ more than once. Nyquist's criterion counts how the loop gain's polar plot encircles $-1$, and so counts right-half-plane closed-loop poles exactly (Razavi, Section 10.8).

blocks.text: Suppose $|\beta H| = 3$ at the phase crossover $\omega_0$. Bode says unstable. But evaluated at $s = j\omega_0$, the closed-loop gain $H/(1 + H) = 3/(1 - 3) = -1.5$ (for $\beta = 1$) is perfectly finite. The instability lives off the $j\omega$ axis: there is some $s = \sigma_1 + j\omega_1$ with $\sigma_1 > 0$ where $1 + \beta H = 0$, a growing exponential. To find such zeros of $1 + \beta H$ we must look at the whole right half plane, not just the axis.
Polar plots and the principle of the argument

A polar (Nyquist) plot draws $H(s)$ in the complex plane as $s$ travels along a path. For $H = A_0/(1 + s/\omega_p)$ with $s$ going up the $j\omega$ axis from 0 to $\infty$, $H$ starts at $A_0$ on the real axis, swings below it (negative phase) and reaches the origin at $-90^{\circ}$. With two poles it arrives at $-180^{\circ}$, with three at $-270^{\circ}$ (passing into the second quadrant). Each pole's phase contribution at a point $s$ is minus the angle of the vector from the pole to $s$; each zero's is plus its angle.

Now let $s$ go clockwise around a closed contour. A pole or zero outside the contour makes its angle swing back and forth with no net change; one inside makes its angle go through a full turn. Hence Cauchy's principle of the argument:

blocks.caption: If the contour encloses $Z$ zeros and $P$ poles of $F(s)$ clockwise, the plot of $F$ encircles the origin $Z - P$ times clockwise.

blocks.text: Apply it to $F(s) = 1 + \beta H(s)$, whose zeros are the closed-loop poles and whose poles are the open-loop poles. Take the contour up the whole $j\omega$ axis and around the right half plane on a huge radius. Then the number of right-half-plane closed-loop poles is $Z = N + P$. For a stable open loop ($P = 0$, true of almost all our circuits), $Z = N$. Encircling the origin with $1 + \beta H$ is the same as encircling $-1$ with $\beta H$, so:

For an open-loop-stable system, the closed loop is stable if and only if the polar plot of $\beta H(s)$ along the Nyquist contour does not encircle the point $(-1, 0)$. Passing through $-1$ means a pole on the $j\omega$ axis, a sustained oscillation.

In practice: plot $\beta H(j\omega)$ for $\omega$ from 0 to $+\infty$; for physical (real-coefficient) systems the negative-frequency half is its mirror image about the real axis; for a strictly proper loop gain the huge right-half-plane arc maps to the origin.

blocks.alt: Nyquist plot near the origin for a three-pole loop gain with two different DC gains. The red curve, for the larger gain, crosses the negative real axis at minus 2, outside the point minus 1, so its closed curve encircles minus 1. The blue curve, for the smaller gain, crosses at minus 0.45 and does not encircle minus 1. Dashed curves are mirror images for negative frequencies.
blocks.caption: Three-pole loop: scaling the gain up stretches the plot until it encircles $-1$.

items: One pole: the plot is a semicircle in the fourth quadrant ending at the origin at $-90^{\circ}$ (and its mirror); it can never reach $-1$. Stable for any $\beta$.
Two poles: the plot ends at the origin from the $-180^{\circ}$ direction but only crosses the negative real axis at the origin. Stable for any $\beta$, matching the Bode analysis.

Three poles: the plot crosses the negative real axis at $Q$, where $\tan^{-1}(\omega_Q/\omega_{p1}) + \tan^{-1}(\omega_Q/\omega_{p2}) + \tan^{-1}(\omega_Q/\omega_{p3}) = 180^{\circ}$. If $|\beta H(j\omega_Q)| > 1$, the point $Q$ lies left of $-1$ and the curve encircles it: unstable. Raising $\beta$ stretches the plot and can push $Q$ past $-1$.

blocks.text: An integrator in the loop puts a pole on the contour itself. Detour around it on a tiny semicircle into the right half plane. As $s$ rounds the detour, $H$ sweeps through a huge arc at infinite radius: for a single pole at the origin, a half-circle clockwise from $+90^{\circ}$ to $-90^{\circ}$ (the mirror of the $\omega \to 0^+$ end joins the $\omega \to 0^-$ end). For $\beta H = K/[s(1 + s/\omega_p)]$ the plot comes in from $-j\infty$, ends at the origin at $-180^{\circ}$, and the big arc closes it on the right: $-1$ is never enclosed, so it is stable for any $K$. Two poles at the origin produce a full circle at infinity, and the stability then depends on whether the finite part of the plot passes left or right of $-1$.

When the phase falls below $-180^{\circ}$ and then rises back above it (for instance with poles and zeros interleaved), the polar plot crosses the negative real axis more than once. Count the net encirclements of $-1$. Such a system can be conditionally stable: stable for loop gains in a middle range, but unstable both if the gain is too high and if it drops too low, for example when an amplifier's gain collapses during start-up or saturation. Bode's 'gain below one at the phase crossover' rule cannot express this; Nyquist's count can. The gain margin and phase margin still have a natural meaning on the polar plot: the distance by which the plot misses $-1$ along the real axis and along the unit circle.

blocks.title: Bode says unstable, closed-loop gain is finite
blocks.text: A loop has $|\beta H| = 3$ at its phase crossover $\omega_0$ (with $\beta = 1$). Compute $H/(1+H)$ at $j\omega_0$ and explain why the circuit is still unstable.
solution: The polar plot crosses the negative real axis at $-3$, left of $-1$, and so encircles $-1$: by Nyquist there are right-half-plane closed-loop poles, at complex $s$ with positive real part, not on the $j\omega$ axis.
blocks.answer: Gain 1.5 at $j\omega_0$, yet unstable: the poles are off the axis.

blocks.title: Critical gain of a three-pole loop
blocks.text: $\beta H = \beta A_0/[(1 + s)(1 + s/10)(1 + s/20)]$ (frequencies normalized). Find the phase-crossover frequency and the largest $\beta A_0$ that keeps the loop stable.
solution: There $|1/[(1 + j\omega)(1 + j\omega/10)(1 + j\omega/20)]| = 0.0289$, so stability needs $\beta A_0 < 1/0.0289 = 34.6$.

blocks.title: Integrator plus pole
blocks.text: Is $\beta H = K/[s(1 + s/\omega_p)]$ stable for every $K > 0$? Use the Nyquist plot.
solution: For $\omega > 0$ the phase goes from $-90^{\circ}$ to $-180^{\circ}$, never beyond, so the plot only meets the negative real axis at the origin.
The detour around $s = 0$ maps to a large arc on the right side, which closes the contour without enclosing $-1$.

blocks.title: Conditional stability
blocks.text: For $\omega > 0$, a loop's polar plot crosses the negative real axis three times: at $-4$ (phase falling through $-180^{\circ}$), $-2$ (rising back) and $-0.3$ (falling again), scaled by the nominal gain. Is it stable at nominal gain, at 40% of it, and at 4 times it?
solution: Each crossing left of $-1$ contributes half an encirclement for positive $\omega$, and its mirror image the other half; crossings in opposite directions cancel. So the loop is stable when an even number of crossings lie left of $-1$.
Nominal: $-4$ and $-2$ lie left of $-1$, in opposite directions: no net encirclement, stable.
40%: crossings at $-1.6$, $-0.8$, $-0.12$; only one lies left of $-1$: unstable.
4 times: $-16$, $-8$, $-1.2$; three lie left of $-1$: net one encirclement, unstable.
Stable for gains below 0.25 or between 0.5 and 3.3 times nominal: lowering the gain into the 0.25 to 0.5 band destabilizes it.
blocks.answer: Stable at nominal; unstable at 40% and at 4 times.
